query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating machine-learning–augmented CALPHAD modeling with ab initio phonon calculations will allow for accurate identification of single‐phase high-entropy alloys exhibiting enhanced local lattice disorder that effectively scatters phonons, thereby reducing phonon thermal conductivity relative to predictions from conventional models.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloys synthesized in their as-cast, single-phase state with high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Application of the new predictive approach to screen the compositional space for HEAs targeted for thermal insulation, selecting candidates whose computed vibrational properties indicate strong phonon scattering.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted under high-temperature conditions within the stability window of the HEAs (e.g., between about 750 °C and 1320 °C) where phase decomposition is minimal.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions arising from multi-element disorder in the high-entropy alloy that create abundant phonon scattering centers.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced chemical complexity disrupts phonon propagation by introducing disorder-induced scattering, thereby lowering the phonon component of thermal conductivity. The predictive approach leverages the interplay between thermodynamic stability and vibrational dynamics to isolate compositions where this effect is maximized.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA compositions identified using the new approach will exhibit roughly 20–30% lower phonon thermal conductivity compared to predictions based on conventional models that do not account for localized disorder effects.
generation.baseline: Current predictive models based solely on standard CALPHAD or ab initio methods which underpredict the impact of multi-element disorder on phonon scattering.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be applicable primarily to single-phase, high-entropy systems. It may not hold for multiphase alloys or those compositions that decompose at the operating temperatures, as the disorder-driven phonon scattering mechanism is intimately linked to the homogeneous atomic distribution in a stable single-phase matrix.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the predicted improvement (20–30% reduction) is uncertain due to the complexities in quantifying lattice vibrational behavior in highly disordered systems, and further experimental calibration is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of high-entropy alloys predicted by the new approach to have low phonon thermal conductivity and a comparable set identified by conventional methods. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature conditions (within 750–1320 °C) and measure their lattice thermal conductivity using techniques such as laser flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (phonon contribution, isolated if possible)
Microstructural characterization to confirm single-phase stability (via XRD, TEM)
Composition verification (using EDS or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured phonon thermal conductivity of the alloys identified via the new predictive approach does not show an improvement (i.e., at least a 20% reduction) over the baseline alloys determined by conventional methods, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available.
